Lightning strikes usually occur during take-off, landing, and passing through storm clouds.
Lightning typically strikes the geometrically extremal points of an aircraft, such as the radome, wing tips, and stabilizers.
The lightning current can reach temperatures of up to 30,000 K in the resulting plasma channel.
Overpressure from the acoustic wave and resistive heating can cause extensive damage to the composite structure, including cracking, delamination, decomposition, and ablation.
The highest lightning current values of up to 200 kA are attributed to small areas like the nose, wing tips, and stabilizers.
The majority of the aircraft fuselage belongs to a zone with lower current levels of up to 2 kA.
The most common lightning current discharges are in the range of 5-10 kA.
The organic conductive composite is manufactured by impregnating carbon fiber reinforcement into a polymeric mixture containing epoxy resin and polyaniline (PANI).
The PANI content is determined based on numerical simulations using percolation theory to balance electrical and mechanical properties.
The organic conductive composite has a significantly lower density compared to composites with metallized fibers or embedded metallic meshes/foils.
The organic conductive composite has a simpler and lower-cost manufacturing process compared to CNT-reinforced composites.
The organic conductive composite's electrical and thermal conductivity properties are comparable to existing LSP solutions based on metallized fibers or embedded metallic elements.
The main industry recommendations for LSP are SAE ARP 5412A and SAE ARP 5414A, which define lightning current waveforms and zoning for different aircraft areas.
The U.S. Federal Regulations and EUROCAE standards in Europe are based on the SAE ARP recommendations.
The regulations cover both direct and indirect effects of lightning strikes, as well as requirements for fuel systems and precipitation static protection.
